walkthroughs.h2: Basic oxides with water and acid
walkthroughs.body_html:
Na2O + H2O -> 2NaOH (pH ~14). MgO + H2O -> Mg(OH)2 (sparingly soluble, pH ~10).

Both react with acids: MgO + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2O. Both contain O^2- ions.

Al2O3 insoluble in water but reacts with both acids and bases.

With HCl: Al2O3 + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2O. With NaOH: Al2O3 + 2NaOH + 3H2O -> 2NaAl(OH)4.

P4O10 + 6H2O -> 4H3PO4 (phosphoric acid, pH ~2). SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4 (pH ~0).

SiO2 insoluble in water but reacts with hot conc NaOH: SiO2 + 2NaOH -> Na2SiO3 + H2O (acidic to base).

Why does first ionisation energy generally increase across a period?
options: Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays roughly constant, so electrons are held more tightly.
Atoms get bigger down a group because nuclei swell when they have more neutrons.
Atoms across a period have more shells, pulling electrons closer.
Atoms get bigger across a period, making electrons easier to add but harder to remove.

mcqs.q: How does a buffer maintain its pH when small amounts of acid are added?
options: A buffer destroys added acid by changing it into water vapour.
The conjugate base in the buffer reacts with added H+ to remove it, keeping pH nearly constant.
Atoms get bigger down a group because nuclei swell when they have more neutrons.
A buffer prevents any H+ ions from being added to the solution at all.

mcqs.q: Why does atomic radius increase down a group?
options: Atoms across a period have more shells, pulling electrons closer.
Each successive element has an additional electron shell, increasing the distance of outer electrons from the nucleus.
Atoms get bigger down a group because they have more protons attracting more matter.
Atoms get bigger down a group because nuclei swell when they have more neutrons.
